newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ exporters want more resources put into SNZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ exporters want more resources put into SNZ.

text.p: An exporters summit group on Wednesday called for more resources to be put into Statistics New Zealand to improve the quality and timeliness of statistics.
The exporters also recommended that Statistics New Zealand, to improve its credibility, calculate and publish the underlying rate of inflation rather than the Reserve Bank.
The group, comprising most New Zealand exporting organisations, had met to find ways to lessen the impact that the maintenance of price stability has on the New Zealand dollar.
Spokesman Malcolm Bailey of Federated Farmers said there were gains to be made from improved statistics but stressed more macro-economic improvements could be made in other areas.

The exporters' wish-list includes reform of the Resource Management and Employment Contracts acts, review of Accident Compensation, removal of tariffs, further privatisation particularly in the electricity industry, abolition of producer board monopolies and deregulation of land transport and water systems.

On the statistics question, Bailey said the 1993/94 underestimation of GDP growth contributed to the failure of the Reserve Bank to dampen down the economy and that had cost millions of dollars and many jobs.
"More accurate data would have got a better response and we would have had smoother growth," said Manufacturers' Federation chief executive Simon Arnold.
The meeting was briefed by Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash and Government Statistician Len Cook.
The exporters said they want imputed housing rentals rather than capital costs to be used in the calculation of housing costs in the CPI.
A decision on review of the index is expected in December.
The CPI should also break down the difference between tradeable and non-tradeable inflation and clearly identify government and local government influences on inflation.
There should be a focus in the inflation data on "policy driven" influences so these were transparent, Arnold said.
He said that while the changes being advocated by the exporters were at the micro level, the group was focussing on the long-term, which was how many of the gains in the 1980s were achieved.
Arnold said exporters expect to get some relief from a falloff in the exchange rate over the next six months.
They saw increased government spending as the biggest problem and they expect fresh inflation pressures in the second and third years of the political cycle.
One ray of hope was Tuesday's announcement of postal deregulation, they said.
"If we had one of those a week then confidence would be restored," Arnold said.
